title: Spectrum
tagline: Explore dispersion, electromagnetic spectrum and scattering of light.

overview.intro: The spectrum of light reveals that white light is composed of different colours and that visible light is only a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum. This chapter covers dispersion of white light by a prism, recombination, properties and uses of different regions of the electromagnetic spectrum, and phenomena such as scattering that explain everyday observations like the blue sky and red sunset.

learn.title: Dispersion and Recombination of White Light

blocks.text: Dispersion is the phenomenon of splitting white light into its constituent colours when it passes through a prism. This occurs because different colours (wavelengths) travel at slightly different speeds in glass and therefore refract by different amounts. Violet light deviates the most and red light deviates the least, producing a band of colours called the spectrum.

The visible spectrum is commonly remembered by the sequence VIBGYOR: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red. If a second identical prism is placed in an inverted position, the dispersed colours can be recombined to form white light, demonstrating that white light is a mixture of colours.

items.text: Prism producing rainbow-like band on a screen.
items.note: Different refractive indices for different wavelengths cause separation.

items.text: Newton’s recombination experiment with two prisms.
items.note: Recombination confirms composition of white light.

blocks.text: In a given medium, red light has the longest wavelength and lowest frequency in the visible range, while violet has the shortest wavelength and highest frequency. Because refractive index varies with wavelength, violet bends more than red in a prism. This variation is the basis of dispersion.

Deviation of a ray by a prism depends on angle of incidence, prism angle and refractive index of the material for that colour. Pure spectrum requires a narrow slit and proper arrangement to avoid overlapping of colours. Understanding which colour deviates more helps in interpreting diagrams and applications.

items: Violet: shortest wavelength, maximum deviation in prism.
Red: longest wavelength, minimum deviation in prism.
Speed of light in a medium depends on wavelength.
A pure spectrum has distinct, non-overlapping colours.

blocks.text: Visible light is part of a broader electromagnetic spectrum that includes, in order of increasing frequency (decreasing wavelength), radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light in vacuum and can exhibit reflection, refraction and other wave behaviours.

Different regions have different properties and uses: radio waves for communication, microwaves for cooking and radar, infrared for heating and remote controls, ultraviolet for sterilisation, X-rays for medical imaging and gamma rays in cancer treatment and industry. Excessive exposure to high-energy radiation such as UV, X-rays and gamma rays can be harmful.

Scattering is the process by which light is redirected in different directions by particles in its path. The amount of scattering depends on the size of particles and the wavelength of light. In the atmosphere, shorter wavelengths (blue/violet) are scattered more strongly by small molecules than longer wavelengths (red).

Scattering explains several natural phenomena: the sky appears blue because blue light is scattered in all directions, while the Sun appears reddish at sunrise and sunset because sunlight travels a longer path through the atmosphere and much of the shorter-wavelength light is scattered away. Very fine particles and larger particles scatter differently, affecting colours observed.

items.meaning: Redirection of light by particles or molecules in a medium.
Separation of white light into component colours due to different refractions.
Band of colours or range of wavelengths produced by dispersion or emission.

blocks.text: Knowledge of the spectrum is applied in communication, medicine, remote sensing and everyday devices. Infrared cameras detect heat, ultraviolet lamps sterilise surfaces, and X-ray imaging helps diagnose fractures. Each application uses specific wavelengths suited to the task.

While electromagnetic radiation is useful, safety precautions are necessary for high-energy regions. Overexposure to ultraviolet radiation can damage skin and eyes, and X-rays and gamma rays require controlled use with shielding. Understanding wavelength-energy relationships helps explain why some radiations are more penetrating or hazardous.

items: Higher frequency electromagnetic waves carry more energy.
Visible light is only a small part of the full spectrum.
Use protective measures against harmful UV and ionising radiation.
Distinguish clearly between dispersion (prism) and scattering (particles).

questions.prompt: The splitting of white light into its constituent colours is called:
questions.answer: dispersion
questions.explanation: Dispersion separates white light into a spectrum of colours, typically by a prism.
questions.commonMistake: Scattering redirects light but does not produce the prism spectrum in the same way.

questions.prompt: In the visible spectrum, the colour that deviates the most in a prism is:
questions.answer: violet
questions.explanation: Violet light has shorter wavelength and is refracted more, so it deviates most.
questions.commonMistake: Red light deviates the least.

questions.prompt: Which electromagnetic waves have the longest wavelength?
questions.answer: Radio waves
questions.explanation: Radio waves lie at the long-wavelength, low-frequency end of the electromagnetic spectrum.
questions.commonMistake: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and highest frequency.

questions.prompt: The sky appears blue mainly due to:
questions.answer: scattering of light
questions.explanation: Shorter wavelengths in sunlight are scattered more by atmospheric particles, making the sky appear blue.
questions.commonMistake: Dispersion by prisms is different from atmospheric scattering.

questions.prompt: Which radiation is commonly used for sterilising medical equipment?
questions.answer: Ultraviolet
questions.explanation: Ultraviolet radiation can kill germs and is used for sterilisation.
questions.commonMistake: Infrared is mainly associated with heat.

questions.prompt: The correct order of colours in the visible spectrum from bottom to top (increasing deviation) is:
questions.answer: ROYGBIV
questions.explanation: Red deviates least and violet most, so in increasing deviation the order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
questions.commonMistake: VIBGYOR is often remembered but represents violet to red.

questions.prompt: Which of the following has the highest frequency?
questions.answer: Gamma rays
questions.explanation: Gamma rays are at the highest-frequency, highest-energy end of the electromagnetic spectrum.
questions.commonMistake: Frequency increases as wavelength decreases across the spectrum.

questions.prompt: At sunrise and sunset the Sun appears reddish because:
options: blue light is scattered away over a longer path
questions.answer: blue light is scattered away over a longer path
questions.explanation: Sunlight travels a longer distance through the atmosphere, scattering shorter wavelengths and leaving more red light to reach the observer.
questions.commonMistake: Scattering is stronger for shorter wavelengths, not longer ones.

questions.prompt: The band of seven colours obtained on dispersion of white light is called the ________.
questions.answer: spectrum
questions.explanation: Dispersion of white light by a prism produces the visible spectrum.
questions.commonMistake: Rainbow is a natural example, but the general term is spectrum.

questions.prompt: Electromagnetic waves with wavelength shorter than violet light are called ________ rays.
questions.answer: ultraviolet
questions.explanation: Ultraviolet radiation lies just beyond the violet end of the visible spectrum.
questions.commonMistake: Infrared lies beyond the red end, not the violet end.

questions.prompt: In a prism, ________ light deviates the least.
questions.answer: red
questions.explanation: Red light has the longest wavelength in the visible range and undergoes minimum deviation.
questions.commonMistake: Violet deviates the most, not the least.

questions.prompt: What is dispersion of light?
questions.answer: Dispersion of light is the splitting of white light into its constituent colours when it passes through a medium such as a prism, due to different degrees of refraction for different wavelengths.
questions.explanation: Different colours refract by different amounts, producing a spectrum.
questions.commonMistake: Mention that white light separates into component colours.

questions.prompt: Arrange the following in increasing order of wavelength: visible light, gamma rays, radio waves.
questions.answer: Gamma rays, visible light, radio waves.
questions.explanation: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and radio waves the longest among these.
questions.commonMistake: Increasing wavelength is the reverse of increasing frequency.

questions.prompt: State two uses of infrared radiation and two uses of X-rays.
questions.answer: Infrared radiation is used in remote controls and in heaters/thermal imaging. X-rays are used in medical imaging to view bones and in security scanning to inspect luggage.
questions.explanation: Each region of the spectrum has applications based on its properties.
questions.commonMistake: Give uses that match the correct type of radiation.

questions.prompt: Why does violet light deviate more than red light in a prism?
questions.answer: Violet light has a shorter wavelength than red light and travels more slowly in glass, so its refractive index in the prism material is higher. As a result, violet light bends more at the prism surfaces and undergoes greater deviation than red light.
questions.explanation: Deviation depends on refractive index, which varies with wavelength.
questions.commonMistake: Relate deviation to wavelength/refractive index, not to colour name alone.

questions.prompt: Describe the electromagnetic spectrum and mention the order of its main regions.
questions.answer: The electromagnetic spectrum is the complete range of electromagnetic waves arranged according to wavelength or frequency. In order of increasing frequency (decreasing wavelength), the main regions are radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. All these waves travel at the speed of light in vacuum and differ in energy and applications. Visible light occupies only a small portion of this spectrum.
questions.explanation: Correct order and the idea of a continuous range are important.
questions.commonMistake: Do not omit visible light or mix up the sequence.

questions.prompt: Explain why the clear sky appears blue and the Sun appears red at sunrise and sunset.
questions.answer: Sunlight passing through the atmosphere is scattered by air molecules and fine particles. Shorter wavelengths such as blue are scattered much more than longer wavelengths like red. During the day, this scattered blue light reaches our eyes from all directions, making the sky appear blue. At sunrise and sunset, sunlight travels a longer path through the atmosphere, so most of the blue and shorter wavelengths are scattered out of the direct path, leaving predominantly red and orange light to reach the observer, making the Sun appear reddish.
questions.explanation: Both observations are due to wavelength-dependent scattering in the atmosphere.
questions.commonMistake: State the role of path length for sunrise/sunset.

questions.prompt: Compare dispersion and scattering of light with respect to cause, conditions and examples.
questions.answer: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its constituent colours due to different refractive indices for different wavelengths in a medium such as a prism. It occurs when light refracts and produces an ordered spectrum (e.g. VIBGYOR from a prism). Scattering is the redirection of light in different directions by particles or molecules in its path, depending on wavelength and particle size. It occurs in media like the atmosphere and explains phenomena such as the blue sky and red sunsets. Thus, dispersion is wavelength-dependent refraction, while scattering is wavelength-dependent redirection by particles.
questions.explanation: Clear distinction in mechanism and examples avoids confusion.
questions.commonMistake: Do not describe the blue sky as dispersion by a prism.

questions.prompt: Why is ultraviolet radiation useful for sterilisation but also potentially harmful to humans?
questions.answer: Ultraviolet radiation has higher energy than visible light and can kill bacteria and other microorganisms, making it useful for sterilising medical equipment and surfaces. However, the same high energy can damage living cells, causing skin burns, premature aging and eye damage with excessive exposure. Therefore, UV is beneficial when used in controlled conditions with proper safety measures.
questions.explanation: Usefulness and harm both arise from the energy of UV radiation.
questions.commonMistake: Mention the need for controlled exposure and protection.

questions.prompt: If a beam of white light passes through a prism, which colour emerges closest to the base of the prism and why?
questions.answer: Violet light emerges closest to the base of the prism because it undergoes the greatest deviation. Violet has a shorter wavelength and higher refractive index in the prism material compared to other visible colours, so it bends more towards the base during refraction at the prism surfaces.
questions.explanation: Maximum deviation corresponds to the path bent most towards the prism base.
questions.commonMistake: Red deviates least and appears farthest from the base.

questions.prompt: A remote control uses infrared radiation while a hospital uses X-rays for imaging. Compare these radiations in terms of wavelength, energy and suitability for their applications.
questions.answer: Infrared radiation has longer wavelength and lower frequency and energy compared to X-rays. Its lower energy makes it suitable for short-range communication in remote controls without penetrating deeply or causing ionising damage. X-rays have much shorter wavelength and higher energy, allowing them to penetrate soft tissues and produce images of bones and internal structures in medical imaging. Because of their higher energy, X-rays require controlled use and shielding to avoid harmful effects, whereas infrared in remote controls is relatively safe for everyday use.
questions.explanation: Application suitability depends on penetration and energy of the radiation.
questions.commonMistake: Link wavelength to frequency/energy trends across the spectrum.

questions.prompt: How would the appearance of the sky change if the Earth had no atmosphere? Explain.
questions.answer: Without an atmosphere, there would be no air molecules or particles to scatter sunlight. As a result, the sky would not appear blue; instead, it would appear dark or black except in the direction of the Sun, similar to the view from space. The Sun would appear as a bright source against a dark background because light would travel directly without significant scattering.
questions.explanation: Scattering by the atmosphere is responsible for the blue colour of the sky.
questions.commonMistake: Base the explanation on absence of scattering, not on dispersion.
